meta.title: Who originally recorded "Everybody's Talkin'"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Harry Nilsson. Fred Neil wrote it and recorded it first, on 13 October 1966, for his self-titled Capitol album — a year and a half before Nilsson's cover.
meta.ogDescription: Not Harry Nilsson. Fred Neil wrote it and cut it on 13 October 1966 for his self-titled Capitol album; Nilsson's 1968 cover became the hit via Midnight Cowboy.

answer.label: Not a Harry Nilsson original — Fred Neil recorded it first, in 1966
answer.sourceLine: Harry Nilsson’s recording is so bound up with Midnight Cowboy that the song is often assumed to be his own. It isn’t. Fred Neil wrote “Everybody’s Talkin’” and recorded it himself, on 13 October 1966, for his self-titled Capitol album — the first recording of the song. The album followed in December 1966, though some catalogues date the LP to 1967. Neil’s version was an album track, not a single, and it passed almost unnoticed; Capitol later reissued the whole album under the song’s title once Nilsson’s cover became a hit.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Capitol Records
original.released: An album track — track six of Fred Neil, cut on 13 October 1966 and issued by Capitol Records in December 1966 (some catalogues, MusicBrainz among them, date the LP to 1967), produced by Nick Venet. Capitol chose “The Dolphins” as the album’s single in January 1967, not this song.
original.charted: Did not chart. Neil’s recording was never issued as a single in its own right.
original.cover: Harry Nilsson’s version, recorded in November 1967 and released on Aerial Ballet (RCA Victor) in July 1968, failed to reach the Billboard Hot 100 on first release. After Midnight Cowboy used it as its theme, the reissued single reached No. 6 on the Hot 100 and No. 2 on Easy Listening in 1969 and won a Grammy.

original.trailTitle: How the record has been traced
trail: Wikipedia’s article on the song states that Fred Neil wrote it, copyrighted it on 20 April 1966, and recorded it on 13 October 1966 for his self-titled Capitol album — Everybody’s Talkin’ ↗.
The album article gives the release as December 1966 on Capitol, produced by Nick Venet, and notes the 1969 reissue retitled Everybody’s Talkin’ — Fred Neil (album) ↗.
MusicBrainz credits Fred Neil as both composer and lyricist of the work — MusicBrainz work entry ↗.

MusicBrainz’s entry for the album carries the 2:58 LP master at track six, but dates that release to 1967 and records no label credit — a caveat against the December 1966 Capitol date given elsewhere — MusicBrainz recording entry ↗.

authors.name: Fred Neil
authors.kicker: The original recording artist — and the writer
authors.heading: Fred Neil
authors.bio: Born Frederick Ralph Morlock Jr. in Cleveland in 1936, Fred Neil became a central, famously reluctant figure of the Greenwich Village folk scene. He wrote “Everybody’s Talkin’” and cut it on 13 October 1966 for his self-titled Capitol album — the song’s first recording. Neil never much wanted the career: he toured rarely, recorded little after 1971, and spent his last three decades in Florida working on dolphin protection, co-founding the Dolphin Research Project with Ric O’Barry in 1970. He died in 2001.

authors.name: Harry Nilsson
authors.heading: Harry Nilsson
authors.bio: Nilsson was a Brooklyn-born singer-songwriter who built a career on studio craft and vocal overdubbing rather than touring. He recorded “Everybody’s Talkin’” for his 1968 RCA Victor album Aerial Ballet; issued as a single that July, it reached only No. 13 on Billboard’s Bubbling Under chart, short of the Hot 100. John Schlesinger then chose it as the theme of Midnight Cowboy, and the reissued single went to No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1969 and won Nilsson a Grammy. The performance is genuinely definitive — the only error is chronological. He died in 1994.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong originator
misattribution.intro: The confusion here isn’t about authorship credit — it’s about who made the record first. Nilsson’s version is so total that the song now carries the subtitle “Theme from Midnight Cowboy,” which leaves little room for the idea of an earlier recording at all.

items.why: His 1968 RCA Victor recording, made famous by Midnight Cowboy in 1969, is the version almost everyone has heard — and is widely assumed to be the first.
Cut on 13 October 1966 for the album Fred Neil, issued by Capitol Records in December 1966 (some catalogues date the LP to 1967). It was an album track, never a single, and it did not chart.
Neil is credited as both composer and lyricist of the song; Wikipedia records the composition as copyrighted on 20 April 1966.

misattribution.truthLine: Fred Neil wrote it and recorded it first, in 1966. Harry Nilsson made it famous in 1969.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question isn’t why Nilsson’s version is famous — it’s why it took a film to make it so. RCA released it as a single in July 1968 and it stalled at No. 13 on Billboard’s Bubbling Under chart, short of the Hot 100. The record hadn’t changed a year later; the context had. Once John Schlesinger laid it over the opening of Midnight Cowboy, the same performance went to No. 6.

Fred Neil’s own recording never had that chance. It sat as track six on a Capitol album by an artist who disliked touring and was already drifting out of the business; the single pulled from that album was “The Dolphins.” The clearest measure of the reversal is that Capitol reissued Neil’s self-titled album in 1969 retitled Everybody’s Talkin’ — the original renamed after the cover that eclipsed it.
detailsBody: 20 April 1966 — the composition is copyrighted by Fred Neil.
13 October 1966 — Neil records “Everybody’s Talkin’,” the song’s first recording.
December 1966 — Capitol Records releases the album Fred Neil, produced by Nick Venet (MusicBrainz and some catalogues date the LP to 1967).
January 1967 — Capitol pulls “The Dolphins” as the album’s single, not “Everybody’s Talkin’.”
November 1967 — Harry Nilsson records his version for RCA Victor.
July 1968 — Nilsson’s Aerial Ballet is released and the single stalls at No. 13 on Billboard’s Bubbling Under chart, short of the Hot 100.
May 1969 — Midnight Cowboy premieres in New York with Nilsson’s recording as its theme.
1969 — the reissued single reaches No. 6 on the Hot 100 and No. 2 Easy Listening; Capitol reissues Neil’s album retitled Everybody’s Talkin’.
1970 — Nilsson wins the Grammy for Best Contemporary Vocal Performance, Male; the recording enters the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999.
context.pull: Same record, one year apart. The only thing that changed was the film in front of it.
